entries.title: How can a cocoon become a silk thread?
entries.answer: A silkworm spins a long strand around itself before it changes into a moth. Layers of that strand form the cocoon. For a kind of silk used in cloth, people gather cocoons and carefully unwind long threads from them. These can be joined into yarn that is often smooth and shiny. Silk fiber comes from a substance a caterpillar can make inside its body. Cotton fiber grows from a plant, so there are very different ways to get the threads that become fabric.
facts: The silkworm that supplies much textile silk is a moth caterpillar.

entries.title: How do tiny fibers become a sheet of paper?
entries.answer: Many kinds of paper start with tiny wood fibers. A mill separates the fibers and mixes them with water, making a wet mass called pulp. It spreads that pulp onto a moving screen. The water drains away while the fibers stay behind and catch on one another. Rollers press out more water, and the sheet dries. Old paper can sometimes be separated into fibers and used again. Shorter fibers or bits of ink can change how the recycled paper looks and feels.
facts: Pressing and drying remove water from a new sheet.

entries.title: How does soap help water wash away grease?
entries.answer: A greasy surface can make plain water form separate drops. Soap changes how these materials meet. Part of a soap molecule gets along with water, while another part gets along with oil. As the surface is rubbed or stirred, soap helps hold broken-up grease in small groups that the water can carry away. There is more to cleaning than making foam. A soapy mixture can carry away oil even where few bubbles are big enough for you to see.
facts: Soap can affect both water and oil because different parts of a soap molecule behave differently.

entries.title: What are the tiny threads in cloth made from?
entries.answer: A cloth can contain thousands of tiny strands called fibers. Some come from plants, like cotton and flax. Others come from animals, like wool from sheep or silk from certain insects. People can also make fibers from manufactured materials. Twisting many fibers together can make yarn. Weaving or knitting yarn can make a piece of fabric. Two shirts may feel different because of the kinds of fibers they use, the way those fibers were made into yarn, and how the yarn is joined.
facts: A fabric tag can tell you what fibers go into a garment.

entries.title: What does a number on plastic tell you?
entries.answer: Some containers have a small number surrounded by a three-sided shape. The number identifies a type of plastic material, which can help sorting. It does not by itself tell you where a container can be recycled. A local program might accept a bottle but have no way to handle an object made with some of the same material in another shape. Labels, food left inside, and mixtures of different parts can matter too. Local recycling rules give the most useful answer.
facts: The code identifies a general type of plastic resin.

entries.title: What happens to old glass bottles in recycling?
entries.answer: A glass bottle can sometimes become part of a new bottle. At a recycling plant the old glass may be sorted, cleaned and crushed into small pieces. The glassmaker can add those saved pieces to the ingredients melted for a new batch. Undesired pieces of pottery, a window pane or a baking dish can have different properties from bottle glass. That is why local collection rules can call for certain kinds of glass, even when all the objects look smooth or clear.
facts: Crushed glass ready to be used as an ingredient is called cullet.

entries.title: What part of a flax plant becomes linen?
entries.answer: A flax plant grows long groups of tough fibers inside its slender stems. After harvest, people loosen and remove other stem material so they can gather those fibers. The long strands can be twisted into yarn and woven into linen cloth. Linen and cotton both come from plants, but their fibers do not grow in the same place. A cotton plant makes its soft fibers around seeds. Flax fibers run along the stem and help give that stem support while the plant is alive.
facts: Linen fibers grow along the flax stem, not on the outside of a seed.

entries.title: Why can an onion make your eyes water?
entries.answer: A knife breaks many onion cells when it slices through their layers. Materials kept apart in an uncut onion can then mix. A few changes happen quickly, producing an onion substance that can travel through the air. If it reaches your eyes, it can irritate them, and your eyes make more tears to clear it away. An onion sitting whole has fewer open cells than a chopped one. That is why cutting the onion makes a bigger difference than simply placing it nearby.
facts: Cutting opens onion cells and lets substances inside meet.

entries.title: Why can salt melt ice on a road?
entries.answer: Ordinary water can freeze at a certain temperature, but water with dissolved salt in it can stay liquid below that temperature. Salt on an icy road can dissolve in small amounts of liquid water at the surface and form salty water. Under suitable conditions, that helps more ice melt into the liquid mixture. How much it works depends on the temperature and how much liquid is available. Salt can also damage plants or move into waterways, so many road crews use it carefully.
facts: Salt cannot melt road ice well in all temperatures.

entries.title: Why can soap make a bubble last?
entries.answer: A bubble forms when air stretches a thin liquid film around itself. Water alone usually cannot keep that delicate film from breaking for very long. Soap makes the film easier to stretch and helps it hold together longer. A floating bubble tends toward a round shape because its film pulls toward the smallest surface it can make around that amount of air. As water drains or evaporates from the film, weak spots can form, and the bubble may pop.
facts: A bubble contains air surrounded by a thin liquid film.

entries.title: Why do some water drops leave white spots?
entries.answer: As rain or groundwater moves through rocks, it can pick up small amounts of minerals. Water with a lot of dissolved calcium or magnesium is called hard water. You usually cannot see those minerals floating in the water. When a drop dries on a faucet or glass, however, some mineral material can stay behind as a pale spot. The spot is a clue that the water was carrying something besides water molecules. Soap may also behave differently in hard water.
facts: Dissolved calcium or magnesium can make it harder for some soaps to make foam.

entries.title: Why does a sliced apple turn brown?
entries.answer: A freshly cut apple has new surfaces where the fruit’s cells meet the air. An enzyme in those cells helps oxygen take part in changes that form brown-colored material. The changes can go faster on a damaged surface than inside a whole apple. Lemon juice can slow the browning for a while because it changes conditions at the wet surface. Browning does not turn the apple into toast. Those two changes look a little alike but happen in different ways.
facts: Crushing or cutting fruit can bring its cells into contact with more air.

entries.title: Why does a wool sweater help keep you warm?
entries.answer: Wool comes from the coat of an animal, often a sheep. Its fine fibers often have little bends or waves. When the fibers are made into yarn and fabric, they can trap small spaces filled with air. Air that stays mostly still can slow the movement of heat away from your body. That helps make a wool sweater feel warm when you put it on in cool weather. The fabric does not have to make extra heat of its own to be useful.
facts: Many wool fibers have a natural bend or wave called crimp.

entries.title: Why does plywood have layers that face different ways?
entries.answer: A piece of solid wood often splits more easily in the direction its fibers run. In plywood, a panel is made by gluing together thin sheets of wood. The grain of one sheet often runs across the grain of the next one. That can keep the whole panel from having one easy direction to split. It can also help the sheet stay flatter when moisture changes. Looking at a plywood edge may show several thin lines where the different sheets meet.
facts: A thin sheet of wood used as a layer is called veneer.

entries.title: Why does soda fizz when you open it?
entries.answer: A bottle of soda holds carbon dioxide mixed into the liquid. Inside the closed bottle, the gas above the drink pushes on the liquid. This higher pressure helps the liquid hold more dissolved gas. Opening the bottle lowers that pressure. Gas begins to leave the liquid, forming bubbles that rise and pop. Tiny rough places in a glass can give the bubbles places to start. When enough gas has escaped, the drink tastes flatter even though much of the liquid is still there.
facts: Carbon dioxide can remain dissolved in a drink even when you see very few bubbles.
